extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate or beginning graduate students in multivariable calculus / real analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and theorems on line integrals, conservative vector fields, piecewise C^1 curves, and Green's Theorem in the plane; includes existence, computation formulas, path-independence criteria, chains, and polygon/annulus examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence Theorem (Theorem 3.44)
rubrics_metrics.description: If γ : [a,b] → R^n is a rectifiable simple arc and F is a continuous vector field on the image of γ, then there exists a unique number ∫_γ F·ds (the line integral) satisfying the usual partition/approximation property (Stieltjes-type approximating sums).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theorem is formulated via approximating sums: for any ε>0 there exists δ>0 such that any partition P of [a,b] with mesh <δ gives the approximating sum within ε of the limit. The integral in this generality is given in terms of a Stieltjes integral (development omitted here; see chapter problems). Uniqueness and existence are guaranteed under these hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reparametrization invariance and orientation sign
rubrics_metrics.description: The value of a line integral is independent of the parametrization as long as the reparametrization is orientation-preserving; if the curve is reversed then the line integral changes sign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If γ1 and γ2 are simple arcs related by a continuous bijection ϕ with continuous inverse and ϕ(a1)=a2 (orientation-preserving), the approximating sums correspond and give the same integral. The reverse arc -γ has line integral equal to the negative of the integral over γ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of line integral via approximating sums / Stieltjes viewpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: Line integrals are defined as limits of sums ∑ F(γ(t_j^*))·(γ(t_j)-γ(t_{j-1})), a generalization of the Riemann integral called a 'Stieltjes integral' in this context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this generality a line integral is not given in terms of an ordinary Riemann integral but via Stieltjes integration; the book omits a full development and refers to chapter problems. The partition/mesh δ-ε formulation is used to define the integral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computational formula (Theorem 3.45)
rubrics_metrics.description: If γ : [a,b] → R^n is a tamely behaved simple arc and F is continuous on the image of γ, then the line integral equals the (possibly improper) Riemann integral ∫_a^b F(γ(t))·γ'(t) dt, interpreting endpoint behavior by a limiting process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The displayed formula includes a limit because γ'(t) may be unbounded near endpoints; customarily one writes ∫_a^b F(γ(t))·γ'(t) dt once the theorem is established. The relation ds/dt = |γ'(t)| is noted; Schwarz (Cauchy–Schwarz) inequality gives estimation tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate in terms of arc length
rubrics_metrics.description: The Schwarz inequality yields the bound |∫_γ F·ds| ≤ ∫_γ |F| ds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for estimating line integrals and for comparing with integrals with respect to arc length; the traditional notation ∫_γ F·ds = ∫_γ F1 dx1 + ... + Fn dxn is noted as helpful for evaluation by substitution dx_i = γ'_i(t) dt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Piecewise C^1 curves and extension of line integral
rubrics_metrics.description: A continuous function γ : [a,b] → R^n is a piecewise C^1 curve if there exists a partition P0 = {c_j} so that each restriction γ|_{[c_{j-1},c_j]} is a tamely behaved simple arc (piecewise C^1 constituents). The line integral over a piecewise C^1 curve is defined as the sum of the integrals over its constituent simple arcs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Piecewise C^1 curves may cross themselves and retrace steps; closed means γ(a)=γ(b) (simple means one-to-one). Additivity holds: ∫_γ F·ds is the sum over constituent arcs. Orientation-preserving reparametrizations leave values unchanged; orientation-reversing flips sign. In diagrams, direction is commonly indicated because of sign sensitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cancellation when retracing occurs
rubrics_metrics.description: If a piecewise C^1 curve contains segments that are reparametrizations of the reverse of another segment, their contributions to the line integral cancel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common in diagrams: when a curve retraces part of itself, the contributions from forward and reverse portions cancel, so they contribute nothing net to the integral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chain formalism for boundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce piecewise C^1 chains as formal sums of piecewise C^1 curves (without regard to order); line integrals extend to chains as sums over constituents and are invariant under a list of allowed operations (subdivision, fusion, reparametrization, cancellation/insertion of opposite arcs, dropping/inserting one-point arcs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two chains are regarded equal if obtainable by the listed operations; if two chains are equal then all line integrals defined on both are equal. Chains can be written with integer multiplicities and compared via common constituents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Region connectivity and existence of piecewise C^1 connecting curves (Lemma 3.46)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any connected open subset U (a region) of R^n: any two points in U can be connected by a piecewise C^1 curve lying in U.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: fix p in U; the set of points connectible to p is nonempty, open (contains balls), relatively closed in U (limits extend by straight segments), hence equals U by connectedness. This ensures path-construction for potential definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservative fields ⇄ path independence (Proposition 3.47)
rubrics_metrics.description: If F is a continuous vector field on a region U, then F is the gradient of a C^1 scalar function on U if and only if line integrals ∫_γ F·ds over piecewise C^1 curves γ depend only on the endpoints γ(a), γ(b) (i.e., path independence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Necessity: if F=∇f then ∫_γ F·ds = f(γ(b))−f(γ(a)) by chain rule. Sufficiency: fix p∈U and define f(x)=∫_{any curve from p to x} F·ds; show this f is C^1 and ∇f=F by local straight-line estimates. The phrase 'line integrals of F in U are independent of the path' = conservative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential existence and mixed partial equality (Proposition 3.48)
rubrics_metrics.description: If F = ∇f for some scalar C^2 function f on U then ∂F_i/∂x_j = ∂F_j/∂x_i for all i,j. Conversely, on R^n (or any star-shaped open set), if F is C^1 and the mixed partial equalities hold everywhere, then there exists a C^2 potential f with F=∇f.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The converse depends on global geometry: it holds on R^n and star-shaped open sets but can fail on regions with nontrivial topology (e.g., an annulus in R^2). Proof proceeds by induction on dimension; construction of f via integrating F1 in x1 then adjusting with functions of remaining variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Green's Theorem — hypotheses (Theorem 3.49 first form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose a region U in R^2 can be described both as the set between two graphs y=f(x) and y=g(x) and as the set between two graphs x=φ(y) and x=ψ(y), with all four graphs piecewise C^1; let Γ be the chain of the four graphs oriented so U is on the left. If P and Q are C^1 on an open set containing U and its boundary, then ∮_Γ P dx + Q dy = ∬_U (∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y) dx dy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The region must admit graph descriptions in both coordinate directions so that both P and Q terms can be handled by the rectangle/graph argument. Each boundary piece must be piecewise C^1 and the orientation must place U on the left when traversing Γ. The proof follows from Example 1 (rectangle) and decomposition arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Green's Theorem — rectangular/example intuition
rubrics_metrics.description: For a closed rectangle R and C^1 functions P,Q on a region containing R, the line integral around the rectangle (counterclockwise) equals the double integral over R of (∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parametrize the four sides appropriately and verify by applying the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus to the integrals along opposite sides; this is the core local idea extended via decomposition or partitions of unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling sets between graphs and necessity of double-graph condition (Example 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Replacing a rectangle by the set between two graphs y=f(x), y=g(x) allows the P-term argument to go through, but the Q-term works for sets that are graphs x as functions of y; hence Green's Theorem as stated requires that the region be representable as graphs in both directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors note this as a subtlety: some sets like the disk are representable in both directions (locally via different parametrizations) which is why the theorem applies; this motivates decomposition/partitioning techniques and the piecewise C^1 hypothesis allowing unbounded derivatives at piece endpoints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annulus and oriented boundary components (Example 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an annulus (region between two concentric circles) the outer circle is traversed counterclockwise and the inner circle is traversed clockwise when putting the region on the left; Green's Theorem applies with this orientation accounting for multiple boundary components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: decompose the annulus into quarters where Theorem 3.49 applies, add results, cancel internal edges; orientation of inner boundary is opposite that of outer boundary. Polar coordinates are convenient for computing the double integral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Green's Theorem for simple closed polygons (Corollary 3.51)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Γ is a simple closed polygon traversed so its inside U is always on the left, and P,Q are C^1 on an open set containing the polygon and U, then ∮_Γ P dx + Q dy = ∬_U (∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y) dx dy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: decompose U into nonoverlapping triangles (via an auxiliary line direction not parallel to any edge) and apply Theorem 3.49 to each triangle; interior edge contributions cancel. The phrase 'always on the left' is intuitive but its precise meaning depends on axis orientation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Piecewise C^1 definition nuance — allow unbounded derivative at endpoints
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition of piecewise C^1 curves is built to allow unbounded first derivatives at the endpoints of each piece (so long as each piece is tamely behaved), to accommodate curves like circles when described as graphs with singular endpoint derivatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors explicitly remark that functions whose graphs had unbounded first derivatives were necessary to handle curves like the unit circle via the graph-method; this is why the piecewise C^1 notion permits such behavior at piece endpoints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smooth manifold-with-boundary context for Stokes generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: For generalizations of Green's Theorem (Stokes' Theorem) it's convenient to work with smooth k-dimensional manifolds-with-boundary in R^n (no corners), allowing use of diffeomorphisms and partitions of unity to reduce locally to the rectangle/upper-half-plane case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This modern geometric approach replaces 'piecewise' boundaries by smooth (C^∞) boundaries and uses singular n-cube machinery; the text points to Spivak's Calculus on Manifolds for details. The need for normals (perpendiculars) and smoothness is emphasized for higher-dimensional surface integrals and area definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of naive surface-area via inscribed polygons
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempting to define surface area in R^3 as the supremum of areas of inscribed filled triangles fails (example: finite cylinder) because sums of areas of certain inscribed triangles can be made arbitrarily large.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This motivates using normals and requiring good surface regularity (smoothness) when defining surface area; hence the higher-dimensional theorems require stronger geometric hypotheses than curve theory did.
